The project

A command center for the modern broker

VitalShield is a vertical B2B SaaS portal for insurance brokers — the people who juggle dozens of clients, tight enrollment deadlines, complex plan comparisons, and constant compliance pressure, all at once. I designed the end-to-end experience: from research synthesis through information architecture to a working, clickable prototype.

My role

Sole UX Designer. I owned research synthesis, IA, interaction design, visual design, and prototyping.

Tools

Figma and Figma Make for design and prototyping. Miro for research synthesis. AI as a design collaborator — to accelerate execution and pressure-test my decisions.

The user

Taylor Morgan — a Chicago-based insurance broker managing a large book of clients.

Who I designed for

Meet Taylor Morgan

The problem

Three pains, heard again and again

I started from research — broker interviews, a persona, a customer journey, and a feature-prioritization exercise. The same three pains surfaced every time:

Drowning in clients and deadlines

Brokers juggle many clients with renewal and enrollment deadlines that, if missed, mean lost coverage and lost trust.

Complexity that loses the sale

Deductibles, out-of-pocket maximums, coverage tiers — jargon overwhelms clients, and the comparison conversation is where deals are won or lost.

Every client is different — but tools force one-size-fits-all

Clients want coverage tailored to their needs. But a broker can't legally rewrite a carrier's filed plan, so personalization has to happen within real, regulated building blocks — a constraint most tools ignore.

These weren't assumptions — each maps directly to interview findings and the journey map.

The low points — the morning triage, the quote comparison, and enrollment — are exactly where I focused. They map onto the Dashboard, the Quotes flow, and Enrollment, and they're why the navigation is grouped by the broker's workflow stages rather than by feature.
The organizing principle

Reduce cognitive load. Automate the deadlines they fear. Make plan comparison so clear the client says yes in the meeting.

Every screen had to earn its place against this.

Designing from evidence

Not designing in a vacuum

Before designing, I studied the broker platforms professionals rate highest — AgencyZoom, EZLynx, Applied Epic, HawkSoft, and Salesforce Financial Services Cloud — and extracted the patterns that separate great broker tools from mediocre ones.

1

The comparative rater is the heart

Enter client data once, compare carriers side by side. The single highest-leverage screen.

2

Think in pipelines, not lists

Leads, renewals, and claims live as visual stages, not flat tables.

3

One 360° client record

Every policy, document, claim, and note in a single view.

4

Compliance enforced in-flow

The best tools gate progress until requirements are met — turning anxiety into a system guarantee.

Information architecture

From 12 scattered destinations to 7 jobs

An early structure had 12 top-level nav items — more than a broker can scan. I consolidated to 7, grouped by the jobs Taylor actually does rather than by feature. Nothing was lost; related destinations became tabs and sub-flows.

Before — 12 items
DashboardLeadsClientsQuotesPlan ComparisonRenewalsEnrollmentClaimsComplianceMessagesReportsSettings
→
After — 7 items
DashboardClientsPipelineQuotesEnrollmentMessagesInsights
Settings (separated)Notifications in top bar
The judgment call: I put Claims inside Clients — a broker thinks "Maria's claim," not "all claims." A dashboard card still deep-links to a global claims view, so both mental models are served without spending a nav slot.

Deep dive · How I think

One component, five rounds

The dashboard's four KPI cards look simple. Getting them right took five iterations — and the journey shows how I work: spot the problem, generate alternatives, weigh tradeoffs, and extract a reusable principle.

v1

Four identical cards

Clean, but generic. Every card wore the same period-over-period delta — even where a trend told the broker nothing useful.

v2–v4

The tension

I tried a per-dashboard comparison dropdown. It was honest but implied every card was a trend, and reframing the whole board buried the urgent work. Consistency vs. correctness pulled against each other.

✕ Rejected
The resolution

One skeleton, two jobs

The health card keeps a trend — sparkline plus a plain-text delta. The three work queues each get a populated detail zone: aging sub-stats, a red/amber/green urgency bar, overdue counts. All four share one skeleton and a one-tap action link, and the period control moved to Insights where trend analysis belongs.

✓ Shipped

A dashboard answers "what needs me now," not "what happened last quarter."

The tradeoff I accepted, stated plainly: the broker loses in-place period switching on the dashboard. I judged row consistency and answering the urgent question first to be worth more.

Deep dive · Domain & ethics

Empowering the broker without letting them fabricate coverage

Personalization was pain #3 — but a broker cannot legally alter a carrier's filed coverage. So I designed "Personalize, not Edit": the broker composes a tailored package from real, carrier-available building blocks, never inventing coverage. Compliance stops being a worry and becomes a guarantee built into the UI.

Locked base plan

Filed figures (premium, deductible, OOP max) are read-only with a lock icon: "Set by the carrier — filed and regulated."

Personalize around it

Only genuinely electable options are interactive — real riders, supplements, and tiers the plan actually offers.

Honest by construction

The UI structurally prevents fabricating coverage. A live total shows base + riders — all real, carrier-filed products.

Good design here isn't just usable — it keeps the broker compliant and the client protected.

Deep dive · System thinking

One signal system, used everywhere

The recurring broker fear was missing something urgent. So I built a single triage language — red means act now, amber means soon, green means healthy — and ran it consistently across renewals, documents, claims, and KPI flags. The same discipline drove the comparison screen: recommendation and selection are two different signals, so they read through different forms, never a shared color.

The most urgent item on any screen is the visually loudest. One signal per item — never competing signals.

Ways of working

AI as a sparring partner

I used AI as a design collaborator — to generate first-draft layouts fast, pressure-test my reasoning, and catch my own inconsistencies. But every decision was mine: I directed the work, critiqued each output against the research and the user's needs, and iterated until it was right. The KPI card took five rounds precisely because I kept rejecting "good enough."

Direct→Generate→Critique→Decide→Iterate↺

Using AI well is a craft. The judgment — what to keep, what to kill, and why — is the design.

The product

The end-to-end portal

From a command-center dashboard to a triage-ready client list, a plan comparison that carries the sales conversation, a compliance-gated enrollment flow, and a renewals pipeline built to stop clients lapsing.

DashboardA command center that answers "what needs me now" — urgent renewals, aging quotes, overdue documents, all triaged at a glance.
ClientsTwo separate filter axes — status and segment — so a broker can find lapsing businesses. Status colors encode one variable; urgency lives in the countdown pill.
Plan comparisonThe sales conversation, made clear — best value flagged per row, jargon explained inline, and a selected state that reads by form so it never collides with the recommendation.
EnrollmentCompliance as a guarantee, not a worry — e-Sign stays locked until every required document is received, with a secure client upload link and a live received / action-needed / awaiting breakdown.
Pipeline · RenewalsRetention, thought of as stages rather than a list — renewals triaged by urgency, premium-at-risk surfaced, competitor intel flagged, and reminder sequences automated so no client lapses unnoticed.

Reflection

What I'd do next

Validate with real brokers

This is grounded in research and competitive patterns, but not yet usability-tested. My first priority: test the Plan Comparison flow with 5 brokers — does the client-friendly view actually help them close in the meeting?

Define taxonomies earlier

I learned to nail down systems like the status taxonomy (Active / At-risk / Lapsing) before designing the screens that depend on them — defining it late caused contradictions I had to chase down.

Measure what matters

If this shipped, I'd track time-to-quote, renewals saved before lapsing, and documents collected on time — the metrics that map to the broker's real pain.

The strongest part of this project wasn't any single screen — it was the discipline of making every decision defensible against the user's real needs.
